01 — The Counsel

Running a business can be the loneliest job in the world. Your team looks to you. Your family worries about you. And the people giving advice have rarely signed the front of a paycheck.

I know the tunnel — the late nights, the numbers that won't add up, the quiet question of whether it's all worth it. I've stood there as an owner, and I still dream up new ventures at 2 a.m.

What I offer is a voice: candid, informed and without bias. No agenda, no upsell, no telling you what you want to hear. I give it to you black and white — then help you think it through, push back where it matters and find the light at the end of it.

I won't tell you to dream smaller. I'll help you decide — and build — with clarity.

02 — The Story

The road so far.

Not a straight line. Every turn became something I now bring to the owners I counsel.

i.
Early Years

Sweat equity

Before any business, there were cornfields and fryers. Detasseling corn under a relentless summer sun and flinging burgers on a packed grill line taught me the hard lessons first: sweat, hard work and perseverance. Show up. Do the work. Finish the row.

ii.
Corporate America

Paying my dues

Years in corporate America — across financial services, autosports, technology, hotel management and sports and leisure — on both sides of the table. I learned the real dynamics between customer and seller, earned a seat in executive-level decision making and helped take new products from idea to market. It's where I learned how business works when the stakes are high and how it truly makes and loses money. It's also where I recognized my abilities and found the confidence to know I could do things better as my own boss.

iii.
Entrepreneur

Behind the lens

It started with a camera and nothing else. From there I built FOTOSPORT into a sports photography, publishing and digital media company — pioneering green-screen, geo-fencing and tethered-camera automated workflows while most shooters were still swapping memory cards. Along the way I learned to be the face and the story of my own brand. The first lesson: nobody hands you a business. You build it.

iv.
The Spark

The moment of decision

Teaching marketing at the University of North Texas, I watched capable students freeze and lose confidence when it was time to decide. It exposed what most business education misses: you can teach marketing, accounting and operations, but without understanding the entrepreneurial mindset — its strengths and its weaknesses — decisions made under uncertainty will fail every time. Building that decision readiness is my life's work.

v.
Professor & Scholar

Teaching founders to decide

As Assistant Professor of Entrepreneurship at Colorado Mesa University's Davis School of Business, I lead the New Venture Practicum and MBA venture courses while completing a PhD on how entrepreneurs build better judgment.

The same frameworks I teach at the undergraduate and master's level — ideation and validation, business models, marketing, finance, operations and decision-making under uncertainty — I now bring directly to founders and owners. University-level rigor, applied to your real business, without the semester or the tuition.

vi.
Now

Founder, researcher, author

Today I turn that research into tools founders can use. As founder of AEON NCI, I created the ENVI™ (Entrepreneurial Neuro-Value Index) Assessment — a 10-domain measure of the entrepreneurial mindset — and the Decision Readiness Index, which show exactly where a founder's judgment is strong and where it will break under pressure. They power Aurora EDU, a decision-training platform for students and faculty, and AEON Dynisis, an inventory and replenishment platform running inside a real retail operation.

I've written a book on the entrepreneurial mindset, my doctoral research studies how entrepreneurship education changes the way people think and I'm now writing Before He Was Wise, a new book on Solomon and how wisdom is formed. The counsel you get is tested on my own work first.

Freedom.
The Why

We didn't start businesses to be chained to them.

Most of us became founders for a reason: to live on our own terms. Adventure. Rest. Time on the river. The freedom to choose how our days are spent.

Somewhere along the way, the business can take over. My work is helping you build a company that funds the life you started it for, not one that consumes it.

Work on your business, not in your business.

The Entrepreneurial Mindset

Ten domains that decide every outcome.

Skills can be taught. Mindset decides whether they get used when it counts.

My ENVI™ (Entrepreneurial Neuro-Value Index) research measures ten domains of entrepreneurial judgment. Each one is a strength in the right measure and a blind spot when it goes unseen. Most founders only discover theirs after a costly decision. Recognizing them first is where better decisions begin.

01

Critical Thinking

Why it matters

Separates signal from noise in markets, data and advice.

If it goes unrecognized

Unexamined assumptions quietly become expensive strategy.

02

Adaptability

Why it matters

Markets shift faster than any plan written for them.

If it goes unrecognized

Rigidity looks like discipline right up until the market moves.

03

Conflict Resolution

Why it matters

Partners, teams and customers will disagree. Growth depends on working through it.

If it goes unrecognized

Avoided conflict compounds into turnover and broken partnerships.

04

Emotional Intelligence: Self

Why it matters

A founder's state of mind sets the tone for every decision and every person in the room.

If it goes unrecognized

Stress, ego and fear drive choices that feel perfectly rational.

05

Emotional Intelligence: Social

Why it matters

Selling, hiring and leading all depend on reading people well.

If it goes unrecognized

You miss what customers and your team aren't saying out loud.

06

Ethical Reasoning

Why it matters

Trust is the one asset that compounds faster than capital.

If it goes unrecognized

Small shortcuts made under pressure become the culture.

07

Execution Discipline

Why it matters

Ideas are cheap. Follow-through is what builds companies.

If it goes unrecognized

Busy starts to feel like progress while priorities drift.

08

Resilience

Why it matters

Setbacks are guaranteed. Recovering from them is not.

If it goes unrecognized

Burnout disguises itself as grit until it doesn't.

09

Risk Awareness

Why it matters

Calculated bets are what separate growth from gambling.

If it goes unrecognized

Overconfidence is the most common bias in high-stakes decisions.

10

Trade-Off Awareness

Why it matters

Every yes is a no to something else.

If it goes unrecognized

Trying to do everything becomes a decision to do nothing well.

03 — The Practice

Let's start with a conversation.

From the first spark to the final handoff, I can help at every phase of the business. Every engagement begins with a complimentary conversation.

How businesses actually move
  1. 01Ideation
  2. 02Discovery
  3. 03Validation
  4. 04Launch
  5. 05Operations
  6. 06Growth
  7. 07Scale
  8. 08Exit

The default path, not a requirement. Invalidation sends you back to discovery. A pivot can send you back to the idea itself.

Recurring decisions · at any point, or never

Capital

Most founders never raise outside money. Funding is a decision you may face many times, or not at all.

Scaling

A deliberate choice, not a destiny. Many great businesses thrive by staying the right size.

Transition

Succession, sale, absorption or closure. How you hand off what you built.

The research behind this model
  1. Levie, J. & Lichtenstein, B. B. (2010). A terminal assessment of stages theory: Introducing a dynamic states approach to entrepreneurship. Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice, 34(2), 317–350. An analysis of 104 published stage models found no consensus on basic constructs and no empirical confirmation of stages theory.
  2. Ewing Marion Kauffman Foundation. (2019). Access to capital for entrepreneurs: Removing barriers. At least 83 percent of entrepreneurs do not access bank loans or venture capital at startup; almost 65 percent rely on personal and family savings.
  3. U.S. Small Business Administration, Office of Advocacy. (2022). Small business finance FAQ. Personal savings is the leading source of startup capital, and 11.3 percent of new employer firms used no capital at all.
  4. U.S. Department of the Treasury. (2025). Financing small business: Landscape and policy recommendations. Only about 0.5 percent of new startups turn to external equity such as venture capital.
  5. Sarasvathy, S. D. (2001). Causation and effectuation: Toward a theoretical shift from economic inevitability to entrepreneurial contingency. Academy of Management Review, 26(2), 243–263. Founders often start from the means at hand rather than a validated idea.

04 — Why Counsel With Me

Not a consultant on the sidelines.

— one

Skin in the game

I've been in the game — building, researching and writing about it. I've failed, made the costly mistakes and learned from every one of them on the way to success. You get the lessons without paying the tuition I did.

— two

A scholar of decisions

My doctoral research asks why capable people make poor calls under uncertainty. That work produced the ENVI™ (Entrepreneurial Neuro-Value Index) Assessment — ten domains of the entrepreneurial mindset, from risk awareness and trade-off thinking to resilience and execution discipline — and the Decision Readiness Index. Together they show where your judgment is strong, where bias like overconfidence creeps in and whether you're truly ready to proceed, revise or pause. I won't tell you what to decide. I'll help you see clearly enough to decide well.

— three

Every seat at the table

Sports, photography, publishing, fashion, music, hospitality, gaming, SaaS, finance and technology. I've built, run and advised businesses across them all, from creative studios to software platforms. Whatever industry you're in, I've likely sat in that chair — and I know what it takes to win there.
